PoK Protests


• At least 7–11 people were killed, with some reports placing the
  toll even higher, as protests raged ahead of scheduled elections over
  economic hardships and political representation In PoK.

• Authorities responded by banning the protest group, filing
  sedition charges, and offering rewards for the arrest of its leaders.

• A recent Pakistan Supreme Court verdict upholding 12 reserved
  seats for Kashmiri refugees living in Pakistan has become the
  immediate flashpoint for the current unrest.

PoK Protests

History and Creation of PoK –

• When British India was partitioned in August 1947, the princely
  state of Jammu and Kashmir had not yet decided whether to join
  India or Pakistan.

• In October 1947, tribal raiders backed by Pakistan invaded the
  state, prompting Maharaja Hari Singh to sign the Instrument of
  Accession with India on 26 October 1947.

• Indian troops were subsequently airlifted into Srinagar, legally
  acceding the entire princely state of Jammu and Kashmir to the
  Union of India.

PoK Protests


• Following Maharaja Hari Singh's accession to India, the first India-
  Pakistan war broke out as Pakistani forces and tribal militias
  attacked the Kashmir Valley.

• The conflict lasted through 1948, with Indian forces
  successfully defending the territory and pushing back the
  invading forces.

• In January 1949, a ceasefire brokered by the United Nations
  brought the active hostilities to an end.

PoK Protests


• On 27 July 1949, India and Pakistan signed the Karachi
  Agreement, establishing a formal ceasefire line supervised by UN
  military observers.

• This ceasefire line temporarily bifurcated Jammu and Kashmir, with
  India getting control of about 65 per cent of the state and
  Pakistan holding the remaining 35 per cent.

• This line eventually became known as the Line of Control (LoC)
  after the 1972 Shimla Agreement.

PoK Protests


• The Pakistan-controlled territories cover about 78,000 sq km and
  came under Pakistani control following the 1 January 1949
  ceasefire.

• The territory is occupied by Pakistan, which has divided it into two
  separate administrative units: Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK)
  and Gilgit-Baltistan.

• India considers the entire territory of the former princely state
  of Jammu and Kashmir, including PoK, Gilgit-Baltistan and the
  Shaksgam Valley, as an integral and inalienable part of India.

PoK Protests


• Gilgit-Baltistan was formed in 1970 as a single administrative
  unit under the name "Northern Areas" by amalgamating the Gilgit
  Agency, the Baltistan District, and the states of Hunza and Nagar.

• In 1963, Pakistan ceded the Shaksgam Valley of Gilgit-Baltistan to
  China in a border agreement, further violating India's territorial
  integrity.

PoK Protests

Political Structure of PoK –

• PoK operates under the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Interim
  Constitution Act, 1974, which was passed by the Legislative
  Assembly of AJK and approved by the Government of Pakistan.

• The Interim Constitution provides for an apparently transitory
  autonomous parliamentary framework, including a President,
  Prime Minister, Legislative Assembly and judiciary.

• The preamble of the 1974 Constitution states that the legal
  status of the territories is yet to be determined and that the
  Constitution is merely a temporary solution pending UN mediation.

PoK Protests


• Under the 1974 Interim Constitution, the executive authority
  of AJK is exercised in the name of the President by the Government,
  consisting of the Prime Minister and Ministers.

• Pakistan has long presented the territory's President, Prime
  Minister, Assembly and flag as symbols of autonomy, but real power
  remains with Islamabad and Rawalpindi.

• The Interim Constitution grants the Legislative Assembly no
  authority over defence, security, currency, external affairs, and
  trade — all key subjects are controlled by Pakistan.

PoK Protests


• Under Article 32 of the Interim Constitution, the Legislative
  Assembly cannot make any laws relating to defence and security
  of the territory, currency, external affairs and trade.

• Historically, much of Pakistan's influence over PoK flowed
  through the Kashmir Council, a powerful institution headed by
  Pakistan's Prime Minister.

• Although constitutional "reforms" in the 1970s altered parts of
  that framework, real authority over key matters continues to rest with
  Pakistan's federal government and military establishment.

PoK Protests


• Politicians, judges and constitutional office-bearers in PoK are
  required to take a mandatory oath affirming support for Kashmir's
  accession to Pakistan.

• This requirement bars alternative political views from entering the
  mainstream and forces representatives to align with Islamabad's
  agenda.

• Unlike Pakistan's provinces, where no such test exists, this
  ideological litmus test ensures complete loyalty to Pakistan's
  position on Kashmir.

PoK Protests


• Under the PoK Constitution, 12 seats in the 53-member
  Legislative Assembly are reserved for Kashmiri refugees
  settled in different parts of Pakistan, including Punjab and Sindh.

• The election of these members happens outside PoK
  geographically as well as operationally, as the local Election
  Commission does not conduct the polling.

• Locals say these seats are effectively used by the federal
  government to get their people into the PoK Assembly, bypassing
  local representation.

PoK Protests


• Apart from the 12 refugee seats, the PoK Assembly also reserves
  five seats for women, one for Ulamas (religious scholars), one
  for Kashmiris living overseas, and one for "technocrats."

• In a House of 53, PoK voters directly elect only 33 people, the
  remaining 20 seats are filled through refugee and reserved-
  seat mechanisms.

• The locals argue that since they do not elect these 20
  representatives, they should not have to pay for them using
  PoK's funds, which fuels the current protests.

PoK Protests

Other Disputed Areas – Hyderabad –

• Hyderabad was the largest and richest princely state in India,
  spanning nearly 83,000 square miles with a population of over 14
  million, comprising present-day Telangana and parts of
  Karnataka and Maharashtra.

• Its ruler, Mir Osman Ali Khan, the seventh Nizam, was then the
  richest man in the world, commanding a fortune that made him an
  important figure in the Muslim world.

• Strategically located in the Deccan heartland, Hyderabad bisected the
  Indian territory like a "dagger poised at the nation's core"; Patel
  famously described it as "a cancer in the belly of India".

PoK Protests


• The Nizam declared his intention to keep Hyderabad as an
  independent sovereign state, neither joining India nor Pakistan,
  and refused to sign the Instrument of Accession.

• In November 1947, India and Hyderabad signed a Standstill
  Agreement, which maintained the status quo for one year,
  during which India would not exercise authority over the state.

• The Nizam, emboldened by Pakistan's Jinnah and hoping for British
  recognition, also made overtures to Portugal for a corridor to the
  sea through Goa, heightening Delhi's suspicions.

PoK Protests


• Taking advantage of the Standstill Agreement and India's
  preoccupation with the Kashmir war, the Nizam's administration
  increased the strength of its irregular paramilitary force called the
  Razakars.

• Led by the fiery orator Qasim Razvi and Maj Gen SA El Edroos,
  the Razakars enforced a vision of Islamic primacy through terror,
  committing looting, abductions, and massacres on Hindu villages,
  displacing thousands.

• The Razakars' belligerence along state borders through cross-border
  raids, coupled with their overtures to Pakistan, made military
  intervention inevitable.

PoK Protests


• On 13 September 1948, India launched Operation Polo,
  deploying about 35,000 troops from Solapur in the west and
  Vijayawada (Bezwada) in the east.

• The Hyderabad state forces numbered less than 25,000, with only
  a fraction being well-trained; the Razakars were ill-trained
  volunteers who proved to be more of a nuisance than a military
  opposition.

• By 17 September 1948, just five days after the operation began,
  the Nizam's forces surrendered, and Hyderabad formally signed the
  Instrument of Accession, becoming part of the Indian Union.

PoK Protests

Junagadh –

• Junagadh was a small princely state in the Kathiawar region of
  present-day Gujarat, with an area of 3,336 square miles, a
  coastline on the Arabian Sea, and a population of approximately
  545,000.

• Crucially, Junagadh did not share any land border with
  Pakistan; it was entirely surrounded by Indian territory and had a
  majority Hindu population of about 80%.

• Despite this, its ruler, Nawab Muhammad Mahabat Khanji III, a
  Muslim of Afghan descent, decided on 15 August 1947 to accede to
  Pakistan, arguing that Junagadh joined Pakistan "by sea".

PoK Protests


• The Nawab's Diwan (chief minister) was Shah Nawaz Bhutto, the
  father of future Pakistani Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto,
  who reportedly saw Junagadh's accession as a bargaining chip for the
  larger prize of Kashmir.

• Jinnah waited for a month to formally accept the Instrument of
  Accession, likely to gauge international reaction and use Junagadh
  as leverage in the Kashmir dispute.

• India refused to accept Junagadh's accession to Pakistan, and
  imposed a naval blockade, cutting off Junagadh's access to the
  sea.

PoK Protests


• Samaldas Gandhi, the nephew of Mahatma Gandhi, formed a
  provisional government demanding accession to India.

• On 25 October 1947, as the situation turned against him, Nawab
  Mahabat Khan fled Junagadh in the dead of night.

• Following the Nawab's flight, India took administrative control of
  Junagadh in November 1947 and, in a move to respect the
  principle of self-determination, agreed to hold a plebiscite.

PoK Protests


• In February 1948, the plebiscite was conducted in which the people
  of Junagadh voted overwhelmingly to join India, with only 99 votes
  cast in favour of Pakistan out of over 200,000 voters.

• Junagadh was subsequently integrated into the Indian Union
  and later became part of the Saurashtra state, now within the
  present-day state of Gujarat.

PoK Protests

Beginning of Protests –

• Residents of PoK first mobilised in May 2023 against rising electricity
  bills, flour smuggling and shortages of subsidised wheat.

• The protests were fuelled by complaints that despite hosting major
  hydropower projects such as the 1,450 MW Mangla Dam and the
  969 MW Neelum-Jhelum project, locals continued to pay
  exorbitant electricity tariffs.

• By September 2023, the Joint Awami Action Committee
  (JAAC) was formed by traders, professionals and activists.

PoK Protests


• In May 2024, protests spearheaded by JAAC escalated dramatically
  over soaring electricity bills and food inflation despite the region's
  abundant hydropower.

• The protests included a long march toward Muzaffarabad, the
  capital of Pakistan-administered Kashmir, which attracted
  widespread attention.

• Pakistan's then Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif responded by
  announcing a package of concessions, including subsidies on wheat
  and electricity and a reduction in flour prices.

PoK Protests


• By August 2024, the JAAC broadened its demands beyond
  economic grievances, calling for systemic political and governance
  reforms.

• The group began demanding the abolition of the 12 reserved
  refugee seats, arguing that these seats gave Islamabad and
  Rawalpindi an additional lever of influence over electoral outcomes.

• The JAAC also demanded that PoK's elected representatives be
  given genuine decision-making authority rather than serving as
  mere extensions of Pakistan's federal government.

PoK Protests


Supreme Court Ruling –

• On 7 June 2026, the Pakistan-administered Kashmir Supreme Court
  ruled that the 12 legislative seats reserved for Kashmiri refugees
  living in Pakistan are constitutionally protected.

• The court held that the refugee seats could not be abolished
  through executive action and that any change would require a
  constitutional amendment by the Legislative Assembly.

• The court also directed that the 27 July 2026 legislative
  elections proceed as scheduled and should not be delayed due to
  the dispute over reserved seats.

PoK Protests


• Following the Supreme Court verdict, clashes erupted between
  police and JAAC protesters in Rawalakot, the capital of
  Poonch district in PoK.

• According to official reports, at least 7 civilians were killed during
  Sunday's clash, while other sources reported 11 people including
  four security personnel died in the violence.

• The clashes resulted in a complete shutdown across PoK, with
  markets closed and normal life paralysed.

PoK Protests


• The Pakistani establishment responded by banning the Joint
  Awami Action Committee as an unlawful organisation.

• The AJK government announced a PKR 10 million reward for
  information leading to the arrest of four JAAC leaders, and
  ordered sedition proceedings against two JAAC figures.

• The government also reinstated 177 FIRs against JAAC
  members, intensifying the legal crackdown on protest organisers.

PoK Protests


• On 5 June 2026, India's Ministry of External Affairs formally lodged
  a "strong protest" with Pakistan over the planned elections to the
  Gilgit-Baltistan Assembly.

• Gilgit-Baltistan has never been made a full province of Pakistan
  because doing so would weaken Pakistan's claim on the entire
  Jammu and Kashmir.

• The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) passes through
  this region, which India has consistently opposed as a violation of its
  territorial sovereignty.

Passage:

In 2026, large-scale protests were reported across Pakistan-occupied Kashmir
(PoK), with demonstrators raising concerns regarding inflation, electricity
tariffs, governance issues, and economic conditions. The protests attracted
international attention due to the strategic location of the region and its
significance in India-Pakistan relations.

PoK forms part of the larger Jammu and Kashmir region, which has remained
a subject of dispute since ______. The region includes areas administered by
Pakistan, while India maintains that the entire territory of the former princely
state of Jammu and Kashmir legally acceded to India in ______. The
developments also renewed discussions regarding the Line of Control (LoC),
regional governance, and socio-economic conditions in disputed territories.

Source: Indian Express

Pakistan-occupied Kashmir is officially referred to by Pakistan as:

A. Gilgit Province
B. Kashmir Autonomous Region
C. Northern Frontier Territory
D. Azad Jammu and Kashmir
ANSWER - D

The Instrument of Accession of Jammu and Kashmir was signed in:

A. 1946
B. 1947
C. 1948
D. 1950
ANSWER - B

The Line of Control (LoC) emerged primarily from which agreement?

A. Tashkent Agreement
B. Simla Agreement
C. Indus Waters Treaty
D. Lahore Declaration
ANSWER - B

The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) is a flagship project
under:

A. Asian Highway Network
B. Shanghai Cooperation Organisation
C. Belt and Road Initiative
D. Asian Development Bank Framework
ANSWER - C

Gilgit-Baltistan is situated primarily in the upper basin of which river
system?

A. Chenab
B. Brahmaputra
C. Indus
D. Narmada
ANSWER - C

Passage:

In 2026, India added its 100th wetland to the list of Ramsar Sites, marking a
significant milestone in the country's conservation efforts. Ramsar Sites are wetlands
designated under the Ramsar Convention, an international treaty aimed at promoting
the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands. The recognition reflects the
ecological importance of wetlands in maintaining biodiversity, regulating water
cycles, supporting livelihoods, and mitigating climate-related risks.

India has witnessed a rapid increase in the number of Ramsar Sites over the past
decade, with wetlands ranging from high-altitude lakes and riverine ecosystems to
coastal lagoons and mangrove habitats receiving international recognition. Wetlands
are often described as among the world's most productive ecosystems and provide
critical habitat for migratory birds, aquatic species, and endangered wildlife.

Source: The Hindu

The Ramsar Convention was adopted in:

A. 1965
B. 1968
C. 1971
D. 1975
ANSWER - C

The Ramsar Convention derives its name from a city located in:

A. Egypt
B. Iran
C. Turkey
D. Morocco
ANSWER - B

Which of the following is not generally classified as a wetland ecosystem?

A. Mangrove swamp
B. Estuary
C. Peatland

ANSWER - D

A. 1975
B. 1980
